items.title: [Real Estate 101 #13] Who Actually Pays Your Agent — and What They Legally Owe You
items.body:
> A real estate agent's job is defined by three documents and one signature: the agreement that hires them, the clause that pays them, and the disclosures that keep everyone out of court.

## 오늘의 개념

Most people meet a real estate agent the way they meet a waiter — someone friendly shows up, shows you things, and a bill appears at the end. That mental model is wrong, and it's the source of nearly every complaint filed with a state real estate commission.

Brokerage practice rests on three pillars.

**1. The agreement that creates the relationship.**
An agent does not represent you because they were nice to you. They represent you because you signed something. On the seller's side that's a **listing agreement**; on the buyer's side, a **buyer representation agreement**. In most states these must be in writing to be enforceable (a consequence of the *statute of frauds*), and they must state a definite expiration date — no open-ended contracts.

Listings come in flavors, and the difference is worth real money:

- **Exclusive right to sell** — the listing broker is paid if the home sells during the term, *no matter who finds the buyer*, including the seller's own cousin. This is the standard listing in the U.S.
- **Exclusive agency** — the broker is paid only if the broker (or another agent) produces the buyer. If the seller finds the buyer alone, no commission.
- **Open listing** — the seller can hire many brokers; only the one who produces the buyer gets paid. Rare in residential.

**2. The compensation clause.**
Commission is *negotiable, always, and by law it has to be.* No state, no association, and no MLS may set or suggest a standard rate — doing so is price fixing under federal antitrust law. What varies is who pays whom, and since the National Association of Realtors' settlement practice changes took effect on **August 17, 2024**, two things changed nationally: offers of compensation to buyer's agents can no longer be published on an MLS, and an agent who is an MLS participant must have a signed written agreement with a buyer *before* touring a home with them. Sellers can still agree to cover the buyer's agent — it's just negotiated in the deal now rather than advertised in the listing feed.

**3. The duties, and the ways agents get sued.**
When an agent represents you as an agent (rather than as a neutral facilitator), they owe **fiduciary duties**: loyalty, confidentiality, obedience to lawful instructions, disclosure of material facts, reasonable care, and accounting for money held. Commissions are the fun part of the job; these duties are the part that generates lawsuits.

The recurring failure modes are boringly consistent: not disclosing a known material defect, practicing law or appraisal without a license ("don't worry, that easement is fine"), sloppy handling of earnest money, and **undisclosed dual agency** — representing both sides without written informed consent. Some states have decided the conflict is unmanageable and banned dual agency outright; Florida and Colorado, for example, use a neutral **transaction broker** model instead. This is why brokerages carry **errors and omissions (E&O) insurance** and why the file — every text, every disclosure, every signed addendum — is the agent's real defense.

## 일상 속에서

Say you're selling a townhouse in Raleigh, North Carolina for **$425,000**.

You sign a 6-month exclusive right to sell listing at a negotiated **5% total commission**, with your listing agreement authorizing you to offer **2.5%** to a buyer's agent if a buyer's agent is involved. At closing:

```
Sale price                 $425,000
Total commission (5%)      $ 21,250
  Listing brokerage 2.5%   $ 10,625
  Buyer brokerage 2.5%     $ 10,625
```

That $10,625 does not go to your agent. It goes to the **broker**, who splits it with the agent under their internal agreement — a 50/50 new-agent split leaves $5,312.50 before franchise fees, MLS dues, marketing costs, and self-employment tax. Understanding this changes how you negotiate: you're negotiating with a business that has a cost floor, not with a person pocketing $21,250.

Now the parts that actually bite.

**Month 4:** your neighbor offers to buy directly. Under an *exclusive right to sell*, your broker is still owed the commission. Under an *exclusive agency* listing, they aren't. One word in a contract you skimmed, $21,250 of difference.

**Month 5:** your agent brings a buyer they also represent. In North Carolina that's legal only with the prior written consent of both parties, and the agent must stop advising either side on price and terms. If they never asked — that's a license complaint.

**Closing day:** you get an email that looks exactly like your closing attorney's, with updated wire instructions and a "please hurry" note. This is the single most expensive mistake in modern residential real estate. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center logs thousands of real estate wire fraud complaints a year, with losses in the hundreds of millions of dollars, and wired funds are often unrecoverable within hours. **Never accept wire instructions by email.** Call the closing office at a number you looked up yourself — not one printed in the email — and verify every digit.

## 3줄 정리

1. An agency relationship — and the duty to protect your interests — begins with a signed listing or buyer representation agreement, not with a handshake.
2. Commission is negotiable by law, paid to the *broker* and split from there; since August 2024 it's negotiated inside the transaction rather than advertised on the MLS.
3. Most brokerage disasters are preventable paperwork problems: undisclosed dual agency, unwritten material defects, and wire instructions verified by phone.

## ✅ 셀프 퀴즈

**Q1.** You sign a 6-month **exclusive right to sell** listing. In month 3 you find a buyer entirely on your own. Does the listing broker earn a commission?
- (A) Yes, the full negotiated commission
- (B) No, because the broker didn't produce the buyer
- (C) Only half, automatically

**Q2. (O/X)** Since the August 2024 practice changes, U.S. real estate commissions follow a standard national rate set by the industry.

**Q3.** Two days before closing you receive an email from your title company with new wire instructions. What's the correct move?
- (A) Reply to the email asking them to confirm
- (B) Call the title company at a number you independently verified and confirm the instructions
- (C) Wire a small test amount first, then the rest

## 📚 오늘의 용어

- **Listing agreement** — The written contract in which a seller hires a broker to market the property, setting the term, price, and compensation.
- **Exclusive right to sell** — The listing type where the broker is paid on any sale during the term, regardless of who found the buyer.
- **Buyer representation agreement** — The written contract hiring a broker to represent a buyer; required before touring homes with an MLS-participant agent as of August 17, 2024.
- **Fiduciary duty** — The agent's legal obligations to a client: loyalty, confidentiality, obedience, disclosure, reasonable care, and accounting.
- **Dual agency** — One brokerage representing both buyer and seller; permitted only with written informed consent in some states, and prohibited in others.
- **E&O insurance** — Errors and omissions coverage protecting brokers against claims of professional negligence or misrepresentation.

---

*정답: **Q1 — (A).** "Exclusive right to sell" means the commission is earned on any sale during the term; a seller who wants a carve-out for self-found buyers needs an exclusive agency listing or a negotiated exclusion clause written into the contract. **Q2 — X (False).** Rates have never been standardized — setting or suggesting a uniform rate is price fixing under antitrust law. The 2024 changes removed compensation offers from the MLS and required written buyer agreements; they did not create a standard rate. **Q3 — (B).** Fraudulent wire instructions arrive from spoofed or compromised email accounts, so replying only reaches the attacker. Verify by voice at an independently sourced number; a "test wire" still sends real money to a criminal account.*

*This is general educational content, not legal advice. Agency rules, dual agency legality, and disclosure requirements are set state by state — check your state's real estate commission before you sign.*

items.title: A Bank Instead of the Dollar: Why Iran Is Racing to Join BRICS's Development Bank Mid-War
items.body:
## A Financial Lifeline Sought Amid Conflict

Even as fighting with the United States and Israel remains unresolved and sanctions continue to squeeze its economy, Iran is pushing hard on a different front: banking diplomacy. Officials at Iran's central bank have said in recent statements that the country's long-pursued membership in the BRICS New Development Bank (NDB) is nearing completion — a move that, if finalized, would give Tehran access to project financing and payment channels that operate outside the U.S. dollar system.

The timing is notable. Most countries pursue multilateral financial memberships during periods of relative stability, when technical and legal groundwork can proceed without geopolitical noise. Iran is instead advancing this bid in the middle of active hostilities, which underscores just how central "de-dollarization" has become to its economic survival strategy.

## What the New Development Bank Actually Is

Founded in 2015 by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — the original BRICS members — the New Development Bank was designed as an alternative to Western-led institutions like the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. It funds infrastructure and sustainable development projects, and increasingly issues loans in local currencies rather than U.S. dollars, a feature that has made it attractive to countries seeking to reduce their exposure to dollar-based sanctions.

Iran formally joined the broader BRICS group as a full member in January 2024, alongside Egypt, Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates. Membership in BRICS itself, however, is separate from membership in the NDB, which has its own governance process, capital contribution requirements and voting structure. Iranian officials have periodically signaled progress on this second, more technical step, framing it as a natural extension of BRICS accession rather than a new initiative.

## Why a Bank Matters More Than a Bloc

For a country under some of the most extensive sanctions regimes in the world, symbolic bloc membership only goes so far. What Iran needs, according to economists who track sanctioned economies, is actual liquidity: financing for infrastructure, energy and trade projects that Western-aligned banks and institutions are barred — or unwilling — to provide.

NDB membership would theoretically open a channel for exactly that. It would also allow Iran to settle at least some transactions with fellow member states in currencies other than the dollar, reducing the risk that payments get frozen or blocked as they pass through the dollar-clearing system, where U.S. regulators have significant oversight.

Analysts caution, however, that the practical impact should not be overstated. The NDB's total lending capacity is a fraction of that of the World Bank, and the bank itself must weigh how closely it wants to associate with a heavily sanctioned member, given its own need to raise capital in international markets where Western investors remain important. Russia's experience — a founding NDB member that has faced difficulty accessing the bank's own resources since 2022 due to compliance concerns among other shareholders — is often cited as a cautionary example.

## A Broader Pattern, Not an Isolated Case

Iran's push fits into a wider trend among sanctioned or sanctions-wary economies to build financial infrastructure that sits outside traditional Western oversight. Russia, China and several Gulf states have all, in different ways, expanded local-currency trade agreements, alternative payment messaging systems, and non-dollar reserve holdings over the past several years.

Whether this amounts to a genuine structural shift away from dollar dominance — or simply a set of workarounds for a small number of heavily sanctioned states — remains a subject of debate among economists. The dollar still accounts for the large majority of global trade invoicing and central bank reserves, and institutions like the NDB remain small by comparison.

## What to Watch Next

The key markers going forward are procedural rather than dramatic: whether Iran's NDB accession is formally ratified by the bank's board, what capital contribution and voting share it is assigned, and how quickly — if at all — the bank moves to approve project financing for Iranian initiatives. Given the bank's cautious posture toward existing sanctioned members, most observers expect any tangible financial benefit to Iran to be gradual rather than immediate, even after formal membership is confirmed.

For now, the story is less about an imminent alternative to the dollar and more about how sanctioned states are quietly building the scaffolding for one, one institutional membership at a time.

items.title: Intel's $20 Billion Stock Sale Draws Over $100 Billion in Demand as AI Chip Race Heats Up
items.body:
## A Bigger Offering, and a Bigger Line of Buyers

Intel has completed an upsized public offering of roughly $20 billion in common stock, pricing shares at $95 apiece, according to reports on the deal. What stood out most wasn't the size of the raise itself, but the appetite behind it: investor orders reportedly topped $100 billion, meaning the offering was several times oversubscribed.

For a company that spent much of the past few years working through a difficult turnaround, that level of demand is a notable signal. It suggests that a broad swath of investors — from large institutions to funds tracking the semiconductor sector — wanted exposure to Intel's stock at a moment when the company is trying to reposition itself around artificial intelligence infrastructure.

## Why Intel Says It Needs the Cash

Chipmakers operate one of the most capital-intensive businesses in the world. Building and equipping advanced semiconductor fabrication plants can cost tens of billions of dollars per site, and the equipment inside them is only getting more expensive as manufacturing processes shrink further.

Intel has indicated that the fresh capital is meant to help it keep pace with demand from AI customers — companies that need enormous volumes of advanced chips to train and run AI models. As cloud providers and AI developers continue to expand their computing capacity, chipmakers across the industry have been racing to expand fabrication capacity, secure supply agreements, and fund next-generation process technology. A large cash cushion gives Intel more room to commit to that build-out without straining its balance sheet.

## The Washington Backdrop

This capital raise doesn't happen in isolation. Roughly a year before this offering, the U.S. federal government took an equity stake in Intel, becoming the company's largest shareholder in the process. That arrangement, tied to broader efforts to strengthen domestic semiconductor manufacturing, marked an unusual level of direct government involvement in a publicly traded U.S. technology company.

That context matters for how investors are reading this latest stock sale. A government stake can be seen as a signal of strategic importance and long-term policy support for domestic chip production. At the same time, it introduces a dynamic that shareholders don't typically have to weigh — the interests and priorities of a government stakeholder alongside those of private investors. Market watchers will likely continue to monitor how that relationship evolves as Intel executes on its AI and manufacturing plans.

## What This Signals About the AI Buildout

Beyond Intel specifically, this deal is another data point in a broader story: the current wave of AI investment is still driving enormous capital flows into chip production. Whether that translates into sustained profitability for chipmakers over the coming years remains an open question that depends on how AI demand evolves, how quickly new manufacturing capacity comes online, and how competitive dynamics with rivals play out.

Investors weighing this kind of news should keep in mind that large capital raises, even when oversubscribed, come with trade-offs — including dilution for existing shareholders and execution risk on the projects the money is meant to fund. As always, developments like this are worth watching as part of the broader picture rather than treated as a guaranteed outcome.

*This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. Readers should conduct their own research or consult a qualified financial professional before making investment decisions.*

items.title: South Carolina First, Iowa Out: Inside the New 2028 Democratic Primary Calendar Shaking Up the Party
items.body:
## A New Order for Choosing the Next Democratic Nominee

The Democratic National Committee has formally signed off on the presidential nominating calendar for 2028, and the headline change is hard to miss: South Carolina, not Iowa, will be the first state to vote. The decision, finalized by the full DNC after months of work by its Rules and Bylaws Committee, closes the book on Iowa's decades-long run as the traditional opening contest of presidential primary season and cements a realignment that began quietly in the 2024 cycle.

For a party that spent nearly half a century sending White House hopefuls first to Iowa's town halls and church basements, the shift is more than a scheduling footnote. It is a statement about which voters the party believes should have the first say in picking its next standard-bearer.

## What the 2028 Calendar Looks Like

According to the calendar approved by the DNC, six states will make up the party's official early window, all voting before Super Tuesday on March 7, 2028:

- **South Carolina** — January 22
- **Nevada** — February 1
- **New Hampshire** — February 8
- **New Mexico** — February 15
- **Michigan** — February 22
- **Virginia** — February 29

That is two more states than were in the early window for 2024, after the Rules and Bylaws Committee voted over the summer to expand the group from four or five states to six, adding New Mexico and Virginia to the mix. Every region of the country recognized by the DNC is represented, a structural requirement the committee set out when it began the selection process in late 2025.

## Why Iowa Lost Its First-in-the-Nation Status

Iowa's removal from the early lineup did not happen overnight. The state's Democratic caucuses had already been pushed out of the top spot for 2024, largely because of the chaotic 2020 caucus, when a reporting app malfunction delayed final results for days and undermined confidence in the process. That episode, combined with long-standing criticism that caucuses draw far fewer and less representative voters than primaries, gave party leaders the opening to rethink the order.

South Carolina's rise reflects a different argument: that the party's early states should better reflect the coalition that actually elects Democrats, including the large Black electorate that has proven decisive in past primaries. Nevada's continued early placement is tied to similar reasoning about racial and economic diversity, along with its strong union presence.

## New Hampshire's Complicated Position

New Hampshire remains in the early window, but not first, which keeps alive a long-running tension between the DNC and the state. New Hampshire law requires its secretary of state to schedule the nation's first primary, a statute the state has enforced for a century. That legal mandate led New Hampshire to hold an unsanctioned primary ahead of the party's approved calendar in 2024, prompting the DNC to strip the state of delegates as a penalty. How that friction resolves for 2028 — whether New Hampshire falls in line with its February 8 slot or again moves earlier on its own — is one of the more closely watched subplots of the new schedule.

## Why the Calendar Matters Beyond the Dates

Primary calendars are rarely just logistics. Going first confers outsized media attention, fundraising momentum and a psychological edge for candidates who can claim an early win. States near the back of the line, by contrast, often see contenders drop out before voters even head to the polls. That dynamic is why fights over calendar order have flared in both parties for decades, and why South Carolina Democrats, who helped revive Joe Biden's 2020 campaign after early losses in Iowa and New Hampshire, have pushed hard to keep their state at the front.

Party officials involved in the process have framed the changes as an effort to modernize a nominating system that many voters and strategists viewed as outdated, while critics argue the reshuffling still leaves plenty of room for future disputes, particularly if states continue to jockey for position or ignore the party's approved order.

## What Comes Next

With the calendar locked in more than a year before voting begins, prospective 2028 candidates now have a clearer map for building early campaign infrastructure, hiring staff and courting voters in the six early states. Expect increased political activity in South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia well ahead of the formal campaign season, as would-be nominees try to establish themselves in the states that will set the tone for the race to come.
